title: Edge-state interferometry as a probe of local flux in isolated quantum Hall systems
authors: Botao Wang, Nathan Goldman, André Eckardt
abstract: Quantum point contacts (QPCs) are essential tools for transport experiments in solid-state systems, enabling the detection of fractional charges and anyonic braiding statistics. Realizing analogous transport setups in isolated quantum-simulation platforms, such as ultracold atoms, remains challenging, since it typically requires coupling to external reservoirs. Here we show that the scattering properties of chiral edge states at a QPC can instead be extracted directly from the stationary edge currents of an isolated, reservoir-free lattice system. Exploiting the sensitivity of this scattering to Aharonov-Bohm-type phases, we propose an equilibrium protocol to detect local magnetic fluxes from ground-state edge currents. We further introduce a dynamical scheme, robust against finite temperature and particle-number fluctuations, based on the post-quench evolution following a sudden potential-bias removal. Since anyonic excitations are themselves associated with a local, quantized magnetic flux, our approach should extend to probing anyonic statistical phases in quantum-engineered platforms.
summary: The authors propose a novel method to measure local magnetic fluxes in isolated quantum systems, such as ultracold atoms, by analyzing edge-state currents at a Quantum Point Contact. They introduce both an equilibrium protocol using ground-state currents and a robust dynamic post-quench measurement. This technique allows for the detection of quantized flux differences and extends naturally to probing exotic anyonic statistical phases.
main_problem: The goal is to probe local magnetic fluxes within isolated quantum Hall systems using edge-state interferometry, circumventing the need for external reservoirs.
main_result: The scattering properties at a Quantum Point Contact (QPC) in an isolated system can be measured by analyzing ground-state edge currents, providing a robust method to detect local magnetic fluxes and probe anyonic statistical phases.
method: Two protocols are proposed: an equilibrium measurement using stationary edge currents or a dynamic scheme based on post-quench evolution following the sudden removal of an initial potential bias.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as an isolated lattice (suitable for ultracold atoms) hosting chiral edge states, described by a Harper-Hofstadter Hamiltonian. The setup involves analyzing transport through a QPC connecting these edge modes.
key_observables: Stationary edge currents ($\langle\hat{j}_\etaangle$), the ratio of left to right edge currents ($j_L/j_R$), and time-averaged current imbalance ($\Delta j$).
important_parameters: Local magnetic flux difference ($\delta\phi = \phi_R - \phi_L$), temperature, and potential bias strength ($V_L$).
main_assumptions: The dynamic scheme is robust against finite temperature and particle-number fluctuations; the analysis relies on relating scattering properties to ground-state currents.
figures_summary:
Figures illustrate QPC setups in open vs. closed systems, showing current distributions related to flux differences ($\delta\phi$). Key figures demonstrate abrupt jumps in current ratios at critical fluxes ($\delta\phi_c$) and show persistent time-averaged current imbalances after quenching a potential bias when $\delta\phi 
eq 0$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by first establishing how edge currents mimic open-system conductance measurements. It then details two measurement protocols—equilibrium and dynamic—showing that both yield measurable signatures dependent on the local magnetic flux difference, culminating in the extension of this technique to anyonic statistics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses implementing complex quantum transport diagnostics (like those requiring external leads) using only internal dynamics within isolated cold atom platforms, making it highly relevant for AMO physicists working with synthetic gauge fields and topological matter.
